questions.stem: On what date did the Australian Constitution come into force and the Commonwealth of Australia begin?
options: 9 July 1900
1 January 1901
26 January 1788
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth was proclaimed and the Constitution took effect on 1 January 1901. The Act containing the Constitution received royal assent in the United Kingdom on 9 July 1900, and the first federal Parliament opened on 9 May 1901.

questions.stem: How did the Australian Constitution become law?
options: It was drafted at conventions in the 1890s, approved by colonial voters and enacted by the UK Parliament
It was written by the High Court in 1901 and then approved by a vote of the first Commonwealth Parliament
It was drafted by the British government alone and imposed on the colonies without their agreement
It was agreed by the colonial governors in 1891 and came into force without any vote by the people
questions.explanation: Delegates drafted the Constitution at federation conventions in the 1890s, voters in the colonies approved it at referendums, and the UK Parliament enacted it in section 9 of the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 (UK). The High Court was created by the Constitution, so it could not have written it.

questions.stem: Which is a main function of the Australian Constitution?
options: It sets the rules of procedure that the NSW Local Court follows in hearing civil cases
It establishes the Commonwealth Parliament, executive and courts and divides law-making powers
It sets out every criminal offence and the maximum penalty for each offence in Australia
It lists all the rights of Australians in a detailed bill of rights that binds every single person
questions.explanation: The Constitution creates the federal system, establishes the three arms of the Commonwealth government, divides power between the Commonwealth and the states and sets out how it may be changed. It contains only a few express rights, and criminal offences and court procedures are set by statute and court rules.

questions.stem: Chapter III of the Constitution, headed 'The Judicature', deals with:
options: the Governor-General, ministers and the executive power of the Commonwealth government
the powers of the states, and how new states may be admitted to the Commonwealth
the High Court and other federal courts, and the judicial power of the Commonwealth
the Senate and the House of Representatives, and the process for making federal laws
questions.explanation: Chapter I covers the Parliament, Chapter II the executive government and Chapter III the judicature. The states are dealt with in Chapter V and new states in Chapter VI.

questions.stem: Why is the Australian Constitution described as entrenched?
options: It can be changed only by the UK Parliament, because the Constitution is a British statute
It can never be changed in any way, because its text was fixed permanently at federation
It can be changed only by a referendum under section 128, not by an ordinary Act of parliament
It can be changed only by the High Court, which rewrites a section whenever a case requires it
questions.explanation: An entrenched constitution is protected from change by ordinary legislation. Section 128 requires a referendum with a double majority, and the High Court interprets rather than rewrites the text. The Constitution has been amended eight times, so it is not unchangeable.

questions.stem: What is meant by the division of powers in the Australian federal system?
options: The courts divide cases between them according to the seriousness of each of the matters heard
Law-making powers are shared between the Commonwealth and the states under the Constitution
Legislative, executive and judicial power are kept in separate arms of the government
The two houses of parliament share the work of reviewing and passing all proposed laws
questions.explanation: The division of powers allocates law-making areas between the Commonwealth and the states, creating exclusive, concurrent and residual powers. Keeping the legislative, executive and judicial arms separate is the separation of powers, a different doctrine.

questions.stem: Which pair are both exclusive powers of the Commonwealth Parliament?
options: Laws about marriage under section 51, and laws about policing under section 128
Laws for the seat of government under section 52, and customs and excise duties under section 90
Laws about education under section 51, and laws about public hospitals under section 109
Laws about the criminal law under section 107, and laws about local councils under section 122 alone
questions.explanation: Section 52 gives the Commonwealth exclusive power over the seat of government and Commonwealth places, and section 90 makes customs and excise duties exclusive. Education, hospitals, criminal law and policing are mainly residual state matters, and marriage under section 51 is concurrent.

questions.stem: Which section of the Constitution preserves the law-making powers of the states that were not given exclusively to the Commonwealth?
options: Section 80
Section 107
Section 128
Section 61
questions.explanation: Section 107 continues every power of a colonial parliament that was not exclusively vested in the Commonwealth or withdrawn from the states, which is the source of residual powers. Section 128 deals with referendums, section 61 with executive power and section 80 with jury trials.

questions.stem: A valid Commonwealth law sets out a complete national scheme for a subject. A NSW law on the same subject adds extra rules that do not directly contradict it. How might section 109 still make the NSW law inoperative?
options: Section 109 applies only where the two laws direct a person to do opposite things, so the NSW law must always survive
The NSW law becomes a Commonwealth law under section 109 and must then be passed again by federal Parliament
The High Court may find the Commonwealth law intended to cover the field, so any state law on it is inconsistent
Section 109 makes every state law invalid as soon as the Commonwealth passes any law on any subject at all
questions.explanation: Inconsistency under section 109 can arise from a direct conflict or where the Commonwealth law is intended to be a complete statement of the law on a subject, known as covering the field. The state law is inoperative only to the extent of the inconsistency, not invalid for every subject.

questions.stem: Under section 122 of the Constitution, what power does the Commonwealth Parliament have over the territories?
options: It may make laws for the territories only about defence and foreign affairs, like its powers over the states
It may make laws for the territories only if a majority of territory voters first approve each law
It may make laws for the government of any territory, including laws that override territory legislation
It has no power over self-governing territories, which hold the same constitutional status as the states
questions.explanation: Section 122 gives the Commonwealth a broad power to make laws for the territories. The Northern Territory and the ACT have self-government only under Commonwealth Acts, so the Commonwealth can override their laws, as it did in 1997 when it overrode the Northern Territory's euthanasia law.

questions.stem: Why do the Northern Territory and the ACT have less constitutional protection than NSW?
options: Their residents cannot vote in any federal elections, while NSW residents vote for both houses of parliament
Their powers come from Commonwealth legislation, while NSW's powers are protected by the Constitution itself
Their parliaments are elected only every eight years, while NSW holds a state election every four years
Their laws are made by the High Court, while NSW's laws are made by its own elected parliament
questions.explanation: State powers are preserved by sections 106 and 107, so the Commonwealth cannot simply take them away. Territory self-government rests on Commonwealth Acts made under section 122, which the Commonwealth Parliament can amend. Territory residents do vote in federal elections.

questions.stem: How does section 96 of the Constitution allow the Commonwealth to influence areas such as education and health that are mainly state responsibilities?
options: It allows the Commonwealth to take over any state department by a vote of the Senate
It allows the Commonwealth to veto any state law within one year of the law being passed
It allows the Commonwealth to appoint the premiers and ministers of each of the states
It allows the Commonwealth to give financial grants to the states on conditions it sets
questions.explanation: Section 96 lets the Commonwealth grant financial assistance to any state on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. Because the Commonwealth collects most tax revenue, tied grants give it influence over state areas, a pattern confirmed in the Uniform Tax Cases.

questions.stem: Under section 51(xxxvii), how can the Commonwealth Parliament gain power over a matter that is not listed in the Constitution?
options: The Prime Minister may declare the matter one of national importance
A state parliament may refer the matter to the Commonwealth Parliament
The Governor-General may proclaim the matter a Commonwealth power
The High Court may add the matter to section 51 in its very next judgment
questions.explanation: Section 51(xxxvii) allows the Commonwealth to make laws on matters referred to it by the parliament of any state, and the law extends only to the referring states and those that later adopt it. No other person or body can add new powers to the Constitution.

questions.stem: In which sections does the Constitution vest legislative, executive and judicial power?
options: Sections 1, 61 and 71
Sections 51, 52 and 90
Sections 7, 24 and 128
Sections 106, 107 and 109
questions.explanation: Section 1 vests legislative power in the Parliament, section 61 vests executive power in the Queen, exercisable by the Governor-General, and section 71 vests judicial power in the High Court and other federal courts. Sections 51, 52 and 90 concern the division of powers.

questions.stem: What is the main reason for separating legislative, executive and judicial power?
options: To prevent power being concentrated in one body, so that it cannot be abused
To make sure every law is passed quickly, with as little debate as is possible
To allow judges to make laws whenever parliament has failed to pass a law
To give the states control over the courts that decide federal matters
questions.explanation: Dividing power among separate arms creates checks and balances and protects individual rights and the rule of law. It does not speed up law-making, and it limits judges to deciding disputes rather than legislating in place of parliament.

questions.stem: Why is the separation between the legislature and the executive in Australia not strict?
options: The executive can override any law passed by parliament if the Prime Minister declares it necessary
Ministers must be members of parliament, so the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature
Judges sit in the Senate and help to make the laws, so the legislature and the courts are very closely combined
The Governor-General chairs every sitting of parliament and votes on all bills passed by both houses
questions.explanation: Under responsible government, section 64 requires ministers to be or become members of parliament within three months. This links the executive and legislature closely, while the judiciary remains strictly separate under Chapter III.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth Parliament passes a law creating a federal court that can both decide legal disputes and set new wages and conditions for an industry. On the reasoning in the Boilermakers' Case (1956), the law is:
options: invalid, because setting wages and conditions is a residual power that belongs only to the state parliaments
invalid, because a federal court may exercise judicial power but not non-judicial power such as setting wages
valid, because the separation of powers in the Constitution applies only to state courts and not to federal courts
valid, because any court may perform any function so long as parliament has passed a law that gives it that role
questions.explanation: In the Boilermakers' Case the High Court held that the Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration could not exercise both arbitral and judicial power, because Chapter III reserves federal judicial power for courts and keeps it separate. The Commonwealth has power over interstate industrial disputes, so the problem is mixing functions, not lack of power.

questions.stem: How does section 72 of the Constitution protect the independence of federal judges?
options: Judges are appointed for a single four-year term, so they cannot be influenced by ministers
Judges can be removed only on an address from both Houses for proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Judges are elected by the people every three years, so they answer only to the voters
Judges may be removed by the Prime Minister whenever one of their judgments goes against the government
questions.explanation: Section 72 provides that High Court and other federal judges may be removed only by the Governor-General in Council on an address from both Houses in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Since a 1977 referendum they must retire at 70. Security of tenure lets judges decide cases against the government without fear.

questions.stem: In Kable v DPP (NSW) (1996), the High Court struck down a NSW law that required the Supreme Court to order the continued detention of one named prisoner. Why?
options: It breached the express right to trial by jury in section 80, which applies to all of the state offences
It dealt with criminal law, which is an exclusive Commonwealth power under section 52
It was passed without a referendum, which every change to criminal procedure requires
It undermined the institutional integrity of a state court that can exercise federal judicial power
questions.explanation: The court held that because state courts can be vested with federal jurisdiction under Chapter III, a state parliament cannot give them functions incompatible with their integrity as courts. Criminal law is mainly a residual state power, and section 80 applies only to trials on indictment for Commonwealth offences.

questions.stem: If the High Court finds that a parliament has made a law outside its constitutional powers, the law is:
options: sent to the Senate to be amended
converted into a delegated regulation
ultra vires and therefore invalid
valid until the next federal election
questions.explanation: A law made beyond a parliament's powers is ultra vires, meaning beyond power, and the High Court declares it invalid. The court cannot send the law back for amendment, although parliament may pass a new law within its powers.

questions.stem: Why can a person not ask the High Court to rule on whether a law is constitutional without a real case?
options: The court can hear constitutional matters only on appeal from the NSW Court of Criminal Appeal
The court decides actual disputes brought by a party with standing, not hypothetical questions
The court may hear constitutional questions only when the Prime Minister formally refers them
The court must wait until the law has been in force for ten years before ruling on its validity
questions.explanation: The High Court exercises judicial power, so it decides real controversies brought by someone with standing, meaning a sufficient interest in the matter. It does not give advisory opinions, and constitutional cases can begin in its original jurisdiction.

questions.stem: What was the main effect of the Engineers' Case (1920)?
options: The High Court held that the states may make laws on any section 51 matter, overriding Commonwealth laws
The High Court held that the Commonwealth may not make laws that bind state governments in any circumstances
The High Court held that the Constitution could be changed by the court without the need for a referendum
The High Court abandoned the reserved state powers doctrine and read Commonwealth powers by their natural meaning
questions.explanation: In Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship Co, the court rejected the idea that areas were implicitly reserved to the states and that governments were immune from each other's laws. Interpreting Commonwealth heads of power according to their ordinary meaning has since tended to expand Commonwealth power.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth ratifies an international environmental convention and passes a law stopping a state from approving a dam in a protected area. Which case most directly supports the validity of this law?
options: The Engineers' Case (1920), on the reserved state powers
Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983), on the external affairs power
The Boilermakers' Case (1956), on the separation of powers
Williams v Commonwealth (2012), on the executive spending power
questions.explanation: In the Tasmanian Dam Case the High Court upheld Commonwealth laws implementing the World Heritage Convention under section 51(xxix), stopping the Franklin Dam. Williams concerned executive spending without legislation, and Boilermakers concerned judicial power.

questions.stem: In New South Wales v Commonwealth (2006), the Work Choices Case, the High Court held that:
options: the corporations power supported national workplace laws for employees of constitutional corporations
the states had exclusive power over workplace relations, so the Commonwealth's laws were invalid
the Commonwealth could regulate workplaces only through the conciliation and arbitration power
workplace relations was a concurrent power only for public servants who work in the territories
questions.explanation: By a majority, the court upheld the Work Choices laws under section 51(xx), the corporations power, which allowed the Commonwealth to regulate the workplace relations of trading, financial and foreign corporations. This greatly widened Commonwealth reach into an area the states had largely regulated.

questions.stem: In Williams v Commonwealth (2012), the High Court considered Commonwealth funding of a school chaplaincy program. What did the court decide?
options: The Commonwealth executive generally needs legislative authority to make such payments, so the funding was invalid
Funding chaplains breached section 116 because it established a religion, so all school funding was invalid
The Commonwealth may spend money on any matter at all without legislation, so the funding was valid
Education is an exclusive Commonwealth power under section 52, so the states could not run chaplaincy
questions.explanation: The court held the payments were not supported by the executive power in section 61 without legislation, which limited the Commonwealth's ability to fund programs directly. Its section 116 challenge failed, because chaplains did not hold an office under the Commonwealth. Parliament quickly passed legislation to authorise such payments.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the effect of High Court interpretation on the division of powers since federation?
options: The court has had little effect, because the division of powers has changed only through successful referendums
Broad readings of heads of power such as external affairs and corporations have shifted power towards the Commonwealth
The court has consistently read Commonwealth powers narrowly, so the states hold more power than at federation
The court has removed the states' residual powers entirely, so every area of law is now exclusive to the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: Cases such as Engineers, the Uniform Tax Cases, Tasmanian Dam and Work Choices expanded Commonwealth power, although Williams shows the court also sets limits. The states keep significant residual powers, and few referendums on powers have succeeded, so interpretation has done more than formal amendment to change the balance.

questions.stem: What is the first step in changing the Constitution under section 128?
options: A bill proposing the change is passed by an absolute majority of the Commonwealth Parliament
A petition signed by one million voters is presented to the Governor-General for approval
The High Court approves the proposed wording of the change in a special hearing
Each state parliament passes the proposed change before the Commonwealth considers it
questions.explanation: The proposed law must pass both Houses by an absolute majority, or one House twice with a three-month interval, and is then put to voters between two and six months later. There is no petition process, and the High Court has no role in approving proposals.

questions.stem: A referendum proposal receives 54% of the national vote, with majorities in NSW, Victoria and Queensland but not in the other three states. What is the result?
options: It fails, because it needs a majority in at least four of the six states
It passes, because more than half of all voters across Australia voted yes
It passes, because the three largest states together have most of the voters
It fails, because it needs a national yes vote of at least two-thirds
questions.explanation: Section 128 requires a double majority: a national majority of voters and a majority of voters in a majority of states, which is four of six. Three states is not enough, however large they are, and no two-thirds national vote is required.

questions.stem: How are the votes of people in the territories counted in a referendum?
options: They count towards the majority of states, with the ACT and NT treated as states
They are not counted, because only residents of the six states may vote
They count twice, once in the national total and once for New South Wales
They count towards the national majority but not towards the majority of states
questions.explanation: Since a 1977 referendum, territory electors vote in referendums and their votes are included in the national total. Only the six states count for the majority-of-states requirement.

questions.stem: Of the 45 proposals put to referendum up to and including 2023, how many were approved?
questions.explanation: Only eight of 45 proposals have succeeded, the last three in 1977. The 2023 proposal for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice, the 45th, was not carried.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum was carried with about 91% of votes in favour and majorities in every state. What change did it make to Commonwealth law-making power?
options: It gave the Commonwealth power to change the Constitution without a referendum
It allowed the Commonwealth to make special laws for Aboriginal people under section 51(xxvi)
It gave the Commonwealth exclusive power over all land in the states under section 52
It allowed the Commonwealth to override state criminal laws under section 109
questions.explanation: The 1967 referendum removed the words excluding Aboriginal people from the race power in section 51(xxvi) and repealed section 127, so Aboriginal people would be counted in the population. It did not change land, criminal law or the amendment process.

questions.stem: In 1999 a proposal to make Australia a republic was put to voters. What was the result?
options: It was withdrawn by parliament before the vote, so no official result was ever declared
It was not carried, with about 45% voting yes nationally and no state majority
It was carried nationally but failed because only three states voted yes
It was carried in every state, but the High Court later found it invalid
questions.explanation: The republic proposal gained about 45.1% of the national vote and did not win a majority in any state, so it failed on both parts of the double majority. A second question in 1999, on a new preamble, also failed.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why so few referendum proposals have been carried?
options: Most proposals have been rejected by the Governor-General after the voters had approved them
A referendum can be held only once every ten years, so too few proposals have been put forward
Proposals without bipartisan support and with unclear details struggle to win a double majority
Voters in referendums are only allowed to vote yes if the High Court has recommended the change
questions.explanation: Successful referendums such as 1967 had support from all major parties, while proposals that divide the parties or leave voters unsure tend to fail, especially given the double majority requirement. There is no rule on how often referendums may be held, and the High Court has no role in recommending changes.
